content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, sheep primarily symbolize God's people (believers, the church, or Israel) in their relationship of dependence on God or Christ as their Shepherd. The image carries connotations of belonging to and being cared for by God, vulnerability and helplessness without guidance, the need for protection and provision, and a tendency to wander or go astray. Believers are the 'sheep of his pasture' who know the Shepherd's voice and follow him.", "primary_basis": ["Psalm 23:1-6 (The LORD is my shepherd)", "Psalm 100:3 (we are his people, the sheep of his pasture)", "Psalm 95:7", "Isaiah 53:6 (all we like sheep have gone astray)", "Ezekiel 34:11-31 (God as shepherd seeking his scattered sheep)", "Jeremiah 23:1-4", "Matthew 9:36 (sheep without a shepherd)", "Matthew 10:6 and 15:24 (lost sheep of the house of Israel)", "Luke 15:3-7 (parable of the lost sheep)", "John 10:1-30 (the Good Shepherd; my sheep hear my voice)", "John 21:15-17 (feed my sheep)", "1 Peter 2:25 (you were straying like sheep but have returned to the Shepherd)", "Hebrews 13:20", "1 Peter 5:2-4"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Christ himself as the sacrificial sheep/lamb led to the slaughter — a Christological reading in which the sheep imagery points to Jesus' atoning death (closely tied to, though distinct from, the 'Lamb of God' motif).", "basis": ["Isaiah 53:7 (like a sheep before its shearers is silent)", "Acts 8:32-35 (Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah, applied to Jesus)", "John 1:29", "1 Peter 1:18-19", "Revelation 5:6-14"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Sheep as the righteous/saved in contrast to goats as the unrighteous/condemned in eschatological judgment (sheep-and-goats separation).", "basis": ["Matthew 25:31-46 (separating sheep from goats at the final judgment)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Sheep as an emblem specifically of national Israel as God's flock, scattered under bad leaders (shepherds) and regathered by God — a corporate-Israel rather than general-believer reading.", "basis": ["Ezekiel 34 (whole chapter)", "Jeremiah 50:6-7", "Zechariah 10:2-3 and 13:7", "Micah 2:12", "Matthew 10:6"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Sheep as emphasizing human sinfulness, foolishness, and straying — the image foregrounds the negative trait of wandering rather than belonging or care.", "basis": ["Isaiah 53:6", "Psalm 119:176 (I have gone astray like a lost sheep)", "1 Peter 2:25", "Luke 15:4-7"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Sheep as sacrificial animals in the levitical cult, symbolizing atonement, offering, and substitution generally (apart from a specific Christological application).", "basis": ["Genesis 22:7-8", "Exodus 12:3-5 (Passover)", "Leviticus 1 and 4-5 (sin and burnt offerings)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Sheep as innocence, meekness, gentleness, or harmlessness of character — e.g., disciples sent out 'as sheep among wolves,' or false prophets in 'sheep's clothing' presupposing sheep as emblem of innocence.", "basis": ["Matthew 10:16 (sheep in the midst of wolves)", "Matthew 7:15 (wolves in sheep's clothing)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Sheep as a pejorative image of mindless conformity or unthinking followers ('sheeple'). This is a modern cultural usage, not a recognized exegetical tradition, though it occasionally colors popular discussion of the biblical texts.", "basis": ["No direct biblical basis; a modern colloquial extension"], "prominence": "rare"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "Sheep is one of the most stable and widely recognized symbols in Christian interpretation: God's people under the care of God/Christ as Shepherd. The alternative readings listed are not so much rival interpretations as context-dependent applications of the same pastoral-flock metaphor (people-as-flock, Christ-as-sacrificial-sheep, righteous-vs-goats, Israel-as-flock). The people-of-God/Good Shepherd reading is dominant across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions, patristic through modern commentary, and in liturgy and hymnody (e.g., Good Shepherd Sunday). Interpreters commonly distinguish 'sheep' (the people) from 'lamb' (the sacrificial Christ), though the two motifs overlap in Isaiah 53 and Acts 8."}
